paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: An ionic bond forms when electrons move from one atom to another, usually from a metal to a non-metal, so that both atoms end up with a full valence shell. The atom that gives up electrons becomes a positive ion, called a cation. The atom that accepts them becomes a negative ion, called an anion.

paragraphs.heading: Table salt as an example
paragraphs.text: Common table salt is sodium chloride. When sodium and chlorine combine, each sodium atom loses an electron and becomes a cation, Na⁺. Each chlorine atom gains an electron and becomes an anion, Cl⁻. The ions then attract one another in a 1:1 ratio, giving NaCl.

paragraphs.heading: Who gives and who takes
paragraphs.text: Atoms whose valence shell is nearly full or nearly empty tend to be very reactive. Strongly electronegative atoms, such as the halogens, often have just one or two empty electron states in that shell and frequently gain electrons to form anions. Weakly electronegative atoms, such as the alkali metals, have few valence electrons and lose them easily to strongly electronegative atoms, forming cations. For elements in the s-block and p-block, the stable arrangement reached is typically that of a noble gas.

paragraphs.heading: Never purely ionic
paragraphs.text: No bond is cleanly ionic: every ionic compound has some degree of covalent bonding, or electron sharing. A bond is called ionic when its ionic character is greater than its covalent character, which means the cation and anion differ greatly in electronegativity. Bonds that are partly ionic and partly covalent are called polar covalent bonds.

paragraphs.heading: Building a lattice
paragraphs.text: The electrostatic attraction between anions and cations builds a solid in which the ions are stacked in an alternating pattern. This structure is called a crystal lattice, or an ionic lattice. In it, separate molecules usually cannot be picked out, so ionic compounds are not molecular. Still, to keep the overall charge neutral, the anions and cations come in strict ratios.

paragraphs.heading: The energy balance
paragraphs.text: Removing electrons to make a cation is endothermic: it raises the energy of the system. When the anion accepts those electrons and the ions attract each other, lattice energy is released, lowering the overall energy. Ionic bonding happens only if the total energy change is favourable. The reaction is usually exothermic, though forming mercuric oxide, HgO, is endothermic.

paragraphs.heading: Strength and properties
paragraphs.text: Ionic bonds are counted among the strongest types of chemical bond. The charge on the ions matters greatly: by Coulomb's law, a salt C⁺A⁻ is held together roughly four times more weakly than C²⁺A²⁻. Ionic compounds generally have high melting points, and the higher the charges, the higher the melting point. As solids they typically do not conduct electricity, but when dissolved in water or melted they break into free ions and conduct well.
